prompt: In the active-passive pair, what is lb2 doing while lb1 is healthy?

choices.text: Carrying half the requests
choices.why: That is active-active; here lb1 carries all of it.

choices.text: Powered off, to be started on failure
choices.why: It is running, and so is its HAProxy; nothing has to start at failover.

choices.text: Running, and serving nothing
choices.why: Right. Configured the same as lb1, and its log printed nothing at all.

choices.text: Answering health checks for lb1
choices.why: Each balancer's keepalived checks its own HAProxy.

prompt: Two balancers run active-active, each at 70% of what one machine can handle. One of them fails. What happens?

choices.text: Nothing visible: the other takes over its address
choices.why: It takes the address, and with it a load it cannot carry.

choices.text: The survivor is asked for 140% and falls over
choices.why: Right. And its own health check fails, so it gives up both addresses.

choices.text: The survivor runs at 70%, as before
choices.why: It now carries its own 70% and the other's 70%.

choices.text: DNS removes the failed address at once
choices.why: DNS knows nothing of the failure, and caches keep the answer anyway.

prompt: With two balancers each kept at a safe load, what does active-active give that active-passive does not?

choices.text: Twice the capacity of one balancer
choices.why: At a safe load each runs at half, which is one balancer's worth.

choices.text: Failover with no gap at all
choices.why: The address still moves by VRRP, with the same kind of gap.

choices.text: Sessions that survive a failure
choices.why: State dies with the machine in both shapes, unless it is stored elsewhere.

choices.text: A spare proven by real traffic every day
choices.why: Right. A passive machine can sit broken for months unnoticed.

prompt: Why did the lab set net.ipv4.ip_nonlocal_bind on both balancers?

choices.text: So lb2 listens on .80 in advance
choices.why: Right. lb2 does not hold the address yet, and its HAProxy is already listening when keepalived brings it.

choices.text: So the balancers accept traffic from outside
choices.why: Any listening socket accepts outside traffic; this is about the address.

choices.text: To let VRRP cross routers
choices.why: VRRP stays on its LAN; this setting is about binding.

choices.text: To hide the real address in the log
choices.why: The log shows the client, 203.0.113.2, whatever this is set to.

prompt: The vrrp_script runs curl -sf against /health every second. What does keepalived read from it?

choices.text: The text of the page
choices.why: -o /dev/null throws the page away.

choices.text: How long the request took
choices.why: A slow answer that arrives passes.

choices.text: curl's exit code
choices.why: Right. 0 passes; anything else, such as 7, fails.

choices.text: The number of web servers up
choices.why: /health knows nothing about the web servers.

prompt: With fall 2, two failed runs of the script in a row put keepalived's instance into the ___ state, and it gives the address up.
hint: It is written in capitals in the log.

prompt: After six requests, lb2's `tail -n 3 /run/haproxy.log` printed nothing. Why?

choices.text: Its HAProxy had crashed
choices.why: It was running; it was the one that took over later.

choices.text: Logging is off on the standby
choices.why: Both have the same file; the log is there, and empty.

choices.text: The laptop sent every request to lb1's own address, 192.0.2.11
choices.why: It sent them to www.example.com, which is 192.0.2.80.

choices.text: It holds no public address, so it served nothing
choices.why: Right. That is the passive half.

prompt: Match each line of haproxy.cfg to what it does.
hint: One of them is keepalived's job, not HAProxy's.

pairs.right: Checks each server with a real request
Sends to the servers in turn

right_distractors: Moves the address to the other balancer

prompt: The last answer before the failure left at 18:11:46.916 and the first after it at 18:11:49.610. How long was the site silent, in seconds?
The first six failures are 0.21 s apart, and the seventh is followed by a 1.213 s pause. What do the two spacings say?

choices.text: The laptop slowed down under load
choices.why: The laptop's loop is the same each time; the spacing comes from the answers.

choices.text: Refused, then unanswered
choices.why: Right. Six were refused at once, since lb1 held the address with nothing listening; the seventh left while the address moved and went unanswered.

choices.text: lb2 answered slowly at first
choices.why: lb2 answered nothing until 18:11:49.610, and then at the usual pace.

choices.text: All seven timed out after a second
choices.why: Then all seven would be 1.2 s apart, not six of them 0.21 s.

prompt: keepalived's log says `Script haproxy_alive now returning 7`. What does the 7 mean?
hint: It is the script's exit status.

choices.text: Seven checks have failed so far
choices.why: It failed once at that point; fall 2 acted on the second.

choices.text: The page answered with HTTP status 7
choices.why: HTTP statuses are three digits; this is curl's own exit code.

choices.text: curl could not connect to the health page
choices.why: Right. HAProxy was dead, so nothing listened on 127.0.0.1:8404.

choices.text: The priority dropped by 7
choices.why: A vrrp_script without a weight does not change the priority; it puts the instance in FAULT.

prompt: The balancer failover took 2.694 s and lesson 15's gateway failover 3.264 s, with the same one-second advertisements. Why was this one faster?

choices.text: lb1 found its own fault and announced it was leaving
choices.why: Right. A priority-0 advertisement lets the backup skip three seconds of silence.

choices.text: The data centre's links are faster than the office's
choices.why: No link in the lab has any delay; the gap is all waiting.

choices.text: lb2 has a higher priority than hq2
choices.why: Both backups have priority 100.

choices.text: HAProxy moves the address itself
choices.why: keepalived moves it; HAProxy only listens.

prompt: A user was halfway through a download through lb1 when its HAProxy was killed. What happened to that download?
hint: What moved: the address or the connections?

choices.text: lb2 resumed it from the same byte
choices.why: lb2 has never heard of that connection.

choices.text: It broke: the connection died with the process
choices.why: Right. The address moves; the connections through it do not.

choices.text: It paused for 2.694 s and carried on
choices.why: Only new connections reach lb2; the old one belonged to a dead process.

choices.text: web1 finished sending it directly
choices.why: web1 was talking to lb1's HAProxy, not to the user.

prompt: HAProxy marked web2 DOWN with `Layer4 connection problem, info: "Connection refused"`. What does that mean?

choices.text: web2 answered with an HTTP error
choices.why: That would be a Layer7 problem; the check never got as far as HTTP.

choices.text: Nothing listened on web2's port 80
choices.why: Right. nginx had been stopped, so the TCP connection was refused.

choices.text: web2 was unreachable on the network
choices.why: A refusal comes from web2 itself, so it was reachable.

choices.text: The balancer refused to check web2
choices.why: The balancer ran the check; web2 refused the connection.

prompt: After nginx on web2 stopped, which of these were true? Choose all that apply.
hint: show stat and the six requests.

choices.text: The backend as a whole was still UP
choices.why: Right. web,BACKEND,UP: two of three servers are enough.

choices.text: Requests went to web1 and web3 in turn
choices.why: Right. Six requests, none to web2.

choices.text: keepalived moved 192.0.2.80 to the other balancer
choices.why: keepalived checks HAProxy, which was fine; a web server is HAProxy's business.

choices.text: Users saw errors until web2 returned
choices.why: All six requests after it were answered.

prompt: All three web servers go down at once. Does the haproxy_alive check make keepalived move the address?

choices.text: Yes, and the other balancer serves the site
choices.why: The other balancer sends to the same three dead servers.

choices.text: Yes, both balancers go to FAULT
choices.why: /health does not depend on the web servers, so neither fails its check.

choices.text: No: HAProxy answers /health itself
choices.why: Right, and on purpose: moving the address could not reach a live server anyway.

choices.text: No, because checks are paused during failures
choices.why: Checks run every second, failure or not.

prompt: A web server's database connection dies, but its home page is a static file. What does `option httpchk GET /` report about it?

choices.text: DOWN, because the application is broken
choices.why: The check asks for a page that works; it cannot see the database.

choices.text: DOWN after a Layer4 timeout
choices.why: TCP connects fine: nginx is running.

choices.text: It depends on the round robin
choices.why: The check runs on every server regardless of the rotation.

choices.text: UP, with a Layer7 pass
choices.why: Right. A check has to request a page that uses the real dependencies.

prompt: An active-active group has 3 members. Following N+1, what is the most each may carry on a normal day, in percent of its capacity, rounded to a whole number?
hint: Two must carry what three carried.

prompt: After HAProxy on lb2 was killed, lb1 showed both 192.0.2.80 and 192.0.2.81. What does that mean for lb1?

choices.text: It now carries the traffic of both
choices.why: Right. The moment N+1 exists for.

choices.text: It is in split brain with lb2
choices.why: lb2 gave its address up; only lb1 holds it.

choices.text: It splits each address's traffic with lb2
choices.why: lb2 has no address left to serve.

choices.text: Clients of .81 must be moved to .80 by DNS first
choices.why: They keep using .81, which now lives on lb1.

prompt: Put the steps of this lesson's active-active failover in order.
hint: The check fails before the address moves.
items: lb2 goes to FAULT and gives up .81
trap: keepalived acts on the second failed check, never on the kill itself.

prompt: A shop keeps each user's basket in the memory of the web server that served them. That server dies. What is the fix that survives it?
hint: Keep the state somewhere that survives the machine.

choices.text: A faster failover of the balancer
choices.why: The balancer was fine; the basket died with the web server.

choices.text: Cookie persistence to the same server
choices.why: It sends the user back to a server that no longer exists.

choices.text: A shared, replicated session store
choices.why: Right. Any server can then serve any user.

choices.text: A third web server
choices.why: More servers, each still holding its own users' baskets.

prompt: A site runs two balancers active-active at 45% each and three web servers at 75% each. One balancer and one web server fail. What breaks?

choices.text: The surviving balancer, at 90%
choices.why: 90% is heavy but within one machine's capacity.

choices.text: The web servers
choices.why: Right. 225% of one server's work over the two left: 112.5% each.

choices.text: Nothing: both layers have a spare
choices.why: Having a spare is not enough if the load does not fit on what is left.

choices.text: Both layers, equally
choices.why: The balancers end at 90%, which fits.

prompt: An engineer changes the keepalived script on both balancers to fetch the home page through HAProxy instead of /health. During a deploy all three web servers are down for a minute. What happens to 192.0.2.80?
hint: Both checks now depend on the web servers.

choices.text: It moves to lb2, which serves the site
choices.why: lb2 reaches the same dead web servers.

choices.text: Nothing: keepalived ignores web servers
choices.why: The new script makes it depend on them.

choices.text: Nobody holds it: both fail their checks
choices.why: Right. Both go to FAULT: the check asks a question the failover cannot fix.

choices.text: It flaps between lb1 and lb2 every second
choices.why: Neither passes its check, so neither takes it.
